subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
vignette: A 54-year-old man is awakened at night by sudden severe pain, redness, and swelling in the first metatarsophalangeal joint of his right foot. He had a large steak dinner and several beers the previous evening. Arthrocentesis shows needle-shaped crystals that appear yellow when aligned parallel to the polarizer and blue when aligned perpendicular. Serum uric acid is 6.0 mg/dL.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout)
Septic arthritis due to Staphylococcus aureus
Gout
Reactive arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis

explanation_correct: This is acute gout: monosodium urate crystal precipitation causing an inflammatory monoarthritis. The crystals are needle shaped and negatively birefringent, appearing yellow parallel and blue perpendicular to polarized light. The classic first MTP joint involvement is called podagra, and attacks are triggered by purine-rich meals, alcohol, trauma, surgery, or dehydration. A normal serum uric acid during an acute attack does not exclude the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pseudogout is caused by rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals (blue when parallel) and typically affects the knee in patients over 50, often with chondrocalcinosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Septic arthritis produces purulent synovial fluid with more than 50,000 WBC/mm3 and organisms on Gram stain and culture, not needle-shaped urate crystals.
explanation_incorrect.D: Reactive arthritis follows a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection and features conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis, without urate crystals in the joint.
explanation_incorrect.E: Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric, erosive small-joint arthritis that is rheumatoid factor positive and does not produce intra-articular urate crystals.

educationalObjective: Needle-shaped negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals in an acutely inflamed first MTP joint establish the diagnosis of gout.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
vignette: A 62-year-old man with hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide for several years develops recurrent attacks of a painful, swollen knee and ankle. Laboratory studies show a serum uric acid of 9.2 mg/dL and mildly reduced renal function. He has no family history of neurologic disease or kidney stones and takes no other medications.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best explains his hyperuricemia?

options.text: Increased purine synthesis due to PRPP excess
Underexcretion of uric acid, potentiated by renal failure and thiazide diuretics
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome from HGPRT deficiency
Increased cell turnover from tumor lysis syndrome
Combined overproduction and underexcretion from von Gierke disease

explanation_correct: Underexcretion of uric acid accounts for about 90% of gout cases. It is largely idiopathic but is potentiated by renal failure and can be exacerbated by medications such as thiazide diuretics, which reduce renal urate excretion. This patient's long-standing thiazide use and mildly impaired renal function fit this dominant mechanism.

explanation_incorrect.A: PRPP excess causes overproduction of uric acid, which accounts for only about 10% of cases and is not the typical thiazide-associated mechanism.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is a rare cause of overproduction presenting in childhood with intellectual disability and self-mutilation, which is absent here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tumor lysis syndrome causes overproduction from increased cell turnover and would be expected in a patient with a high-grade malignancy under treatment.
explanation_incorrect.E: Alcohol use and von Gierke disease produce a combined mechanism, but there is no history of alcohol abuse or glycogen storage disease in this patient.

educationalObjective: Underexcretion of uric acid is the dominant mechanism of hyperuricemia and is worsened by renal failure and thiazide diuretics.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
vignette: A 4-year-old boy has severe intellectual disability, spastic quadriparesis, and a compulsive habit of biting his fingers and lips. Laboratory studies show marked hyperuricemia with increased urinary uric acid excretion. His renal function is normal and he takes no diuretics or other medications.
question: Which of the following best categorizes the mechanism of his hyperuricemia?

options.text: Idiopathic underexcretion of uric acid by the kidney
Underexcretion caused by chronic thiazide use
Underexcretion caused by chronic kidney disease
Overproduction of uric acid due to HGPRT deficiency
Combined overproduction and underexcretion due to alcohol use

explanation_correct: This child has Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). Failure of the purine salvage pathway raises PRPP and drives de novo purine synthesis, causing overproduction of uric acid. Overproduction accounts for roughly 10% of gout and is suggested here by hyperuricosuria, neurologic impairment, and self-mutilation in early childhood.

explanation_incorrect.A: Idiopathic underexcretion is the majority mechanism of gout but has no associated neurologic findings or marked hyperuricosuria in a toddler.
explanation_incorrect.B: Thiazide diuretics cause underexcretion; this child takes no diuretics and has neurologic signs inconsistent with a drug effect.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chronic kidney disease causes underexcretion, but renal function is normal and uric acid excretion is increased rather than reduced.
explanation_incorrect.E: Alcohol use and von Gierke disease cause a combined mechanism; there is no alcohol exposure and the age and neurologic picture point to an inherited enzyme defect.

educationalObjective: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome causes hyperuricemia through overproduction of uric acid from HGPRT deficiency and failed purine salvage.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
vignette: A 48-year-old man presents with an acute, exquisitely tender, erythematous first MTP joint. Arthrocentesis demonstrates needle-shaped crystals that are yellow parallel and blue perpendicular to polarized light. His serum uric acid measured during the attack is 5.2 mg/dL, which is within the normal range, and he takes no urate-lowering medication.
question: Which of the following best explains this laboratory finding?

options.text: Serum uric acid may be normal during an acute attack as urate shifts out of the circulation and into the inflamed joint
The crystals are actually calcium pyrophosphate, so serum uric acid is not relevant
The normal value indicates underlying renal failure with reduced urate synthesis
It proves the diagnosis is septic arthritis rather than gout
Serum uric acid is always low in patients who have developed tophi

explanation_correct: During an acute gout attack, urate precipitates into the joint and inflammatory changes can lower or normalize the measured serum uric acid. A normal serum uric acid therefore does not exclude gout when typical needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals are identified. The crystal analysis, not the serum value, establishes the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent, appearing blue when parallel, whereas these crystals are needle shaped and negative.
explanation_incorrect.C: Renal failure reduces urate excretion and would tend to raise, not normalize, serum uric acid; it does not reduce urate synthesis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Septic arthritis yields purulent fluid with more than 50,000 WBC/mm3 and organisms, not needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tophi are deposits of monosodium urate and are associated with chronic hyperuricemia, not an invariable low serum uric acid.

educationalObjective: A normal serum uric acid during an acute gout flare does not rule out gout when characteristic urate crystals are present in synovial fluid.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
vignette: A 60-year-old man with 15 years of poorly controlled gout has developed firm, yellow-white, chalky nodules. One is located on the external ear, another overlies the olecranon bursa, and a third is found along the Achilles tendon. They are nontender but have slowly enlarged.
question: Which of the following best describes these nodules?

options.text: Heberden nodes of osteoarthritis
Bouchard nodes of osteoarthritis
Rheumatoid nodules
Erythema nodosum
Tophi composed of deposited monosodium urate crystals

explanation_correct: Tophi are chalky deposits of monosodium urate crystals that develop in chronic gout. Classic locations include the external ear, olecranon bursa, and Achilles tendon. Their presence reflects long-standing hyperuricemia and recurrent crystal deposition.

explanation_incorrect.A: Heberden nodes are bony enlargements of the distal interphalangeal joints in osteoarthritis, not chalky periarticular deposits.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bouchard nodes are bony enlargements of the proximal interphalangeal joints in osteoarthritis and are not composed of urate.
explanation_incorrect.C: Rheumatoid nodules are firm subcutaneous nodules associated with rheumatoid arthritis and rheumatoid factor, not deposits of monosodium urate.
explanation_incorrect.D: Erythema nodosum presents as tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules classically over the shins, not on the ear or Achilles tendon.

educationalObjective: Tophi are monosodium urate deposits of chronic gout with a classic distribution including the external ear, olecranon bursa, and Achilles tendon.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
vignette: A 55-year-old man with gout presents with an acute, painful, swollen knee and is treated for the flare. Once the attack resolves, his physician plans chronic preventive therapy. A 24-hour urine collection shows high urinary uric acid excretion, identifying him as an overproducer of uric acid.
question: Which of the following pairs best matches an acute abortive treatment and an appropriate chronic preventive agent for this patient?

options.text: Indomethacin for acute attacks; probenecid for chronic prevention in this overproducer
Indomethacin for acute attacks; allopurinol for chronic prevention in this overproducer
Allopurinol for acute attacks; colchicine for chronic prevention
Colchicine for acute attacks; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for chronic prevention
Probenecid for acute attacks; glucocorticoids for chronic prevention

explanation_correct: Acute gout is treated with NSAIDs such as indomethacin, glucocorticoids, or colchicine. Chronic prevention uses allopurinol or probenecid. For an overproducer with high urinary uric acid, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor such as allopurinol is preferred because it reduces uric acid production rather than increasing renal excretion.

explanation_incorrect.A: Probenecid is a uricosuric that increases renal urate excretion and is better suited to underexcretors than to overproducers with high urinary uric acid.
explanation_incorrect.C: Allopurinol is not used to abort an acute attack; starting urate-lowering therapy during a flare can prolong or worsen the inflammation.
explanation_incorrect.D: NSAIDs are acute abortive agents and are not the standard chronic preventive monotherapy for gout.
explanation_incorrect.E: Probenecid is not an acute treatment, and glucocorticoids are used for acute flares rather than long-term prevention.

educationalObjective: Acute gout is treated with NSAIDs, colchicine, or steroids, while chronic prevention in an overproducer favors a xanthine oxidase inhibitor such as allopurinol.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
vignette: A 68-year-old woman presents with acute pain, warmth, and swelling of the right knee. Radiographs show linear calcification within the articular cartilage. Arthrocentesis reveals rhomboid-shaped crystals that appear blue when aligned parallel to the polarizer and weakly positively birefringent.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Gout
Septic arthritis
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout)
Osteoarthritis
Reactive arthritis

explanation_correct: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) occurs in patients over 50 and most often affects the knee. Crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent, appearing blue when parallel to the polarizer. Chondrocalcinosis, or cartilage calcification on radiograph, supports the diagnosis. Acute treatment includes NSAIDs, colchicine, and glucocorticoids, with colchicine used for prophylaxis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Gout crystals are needle shaped and negatively birefringent, appearing yellow parallel and blue perpendicular, not rhomboid and blue parallel.
explanation_incorrect.B: Septic arthritis produces purulent synovial fluid with more than 50,000 WBC/mm3 and a positive Gram stain or culture rather than rhomboid crystals.
explanation_incorrect.D: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease without acute crystal-induced inflammation or chondrocalcinosis as the defining feature.
explanation_incorrect.E: Reactive arthritis follows an infection and includes conjunctivitis and urethritis; it does not feature calcium pyrophosphate crystals.

educationalObjective: Rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals with chondrocalcinosis in an older patient's knee identify pseudogout, the blue P's of CPPD.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
vignette: A 58-year-old man with recurrent attacks of painful knee swelling has synovial fluid containing rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals. He also has bronze pigmentation of the skin, diabetes mellitus, and cirrhosis. His ferritin is markedly elevated.
question: Which of the following underlying conditions is most strongly associated with this patient's crystal arthropathy?

options.text: Hyperuricemia from underexcretion of uric acid
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
Sickle cell disease
Hemochromatosis
Rheumatoid arthritis

explanation_correct: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease is sometimes associated with hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and joint trauma. This patient's bronze skin, diabetes, cirrhosis, and high ferritin indicate hemochromatosis. The rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals fit CPPD, summarized by the blue P's: blue when parallel, positive birefringence, calcium pyrophosphate, and pseudogout.

explanation_incorrect.A: Underexcretion hyperuricemia produces gout with needle-shaped negatively birefringent urate crystals, not rhomboid positively birefringent crystals.
explanation_incorrect.B: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome causes overproduction gout in childhood with neurologic features, not adult-onset CPPD.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sickle cell disease predisposes to Salmonella osteomyelitis and vaso-occlusive pain crises, not calcium pyrophosphate deposition.
explanation_incorrect.E: Rheumatoid arthritis is a seropositive erosive polyarthritis and is not a recognized association of CPPD crystal deposition.

educationalObjective: CPPD is associated with hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and joint trauma, and its crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.
